records.current_summary:
For a trans traveler the practical difference in Kebbi is jurisdictional: it runs a parallel religious criminal code - in operation since 1 December 2000 - that applies to Muslims, with death by stoning as the maximum for men's same-sex acts and up to 50 lashes with imprisonment for up to six months for same-sex acts between women; the June 2025 government note confirms the code remains in force.

Practical safety: for a Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor who is outed, exposure is to a religious court applying a criminal code broader in scope and harsher in penalty than the national statute alone - the code extends criminalisation to acts between women that the national law does not reach; no enforcement record against trans people specific to this state/province exists.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Nigeria (Wikipedia) - Shari'a-state penalty context for Kebbi
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Nigeria' (fetched in full via MediaWiki API, cached research/fetched/815928c9a45eeba4.txt) situates Kebbi inside the northern Shari'a block: in Shari'a-governed northern states punishments for same-sex acts range from imprisonment to capital punishment, and lesbianism is punishable by imprisonment or caning in most states with death penalties applied only in Kano and Katsina - i.e., Kebbi sits on the lashing/imprisonment tier rather than the capital tier, consistent with the record's own statute reading. It also documents the cross-dressing layer (prison or fine for men who dress or behave as women; Kano 2025 one-year imprisonment sentence). Placement axis: nothing on where trans prisoners are housed - no housing, segregation or placement rule for Kebbi or Nigeria anywhere in the article.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in Nigeria (Wikipedia) - criminalisation and trans visibility
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia article (fetched in full via MediaWiki API, cached research/fetched/767cdbb3294908bd.txt) covering the community-facing picture: the Criminal Code criminalises sex acts between men with penalties up to 14 years' imprisonment, gross indecency between men up to 3 years, lesbianism punishable by imprisonment or caning in most states with death in Kano and Katsina, and cross-dressing penalised in some states (Kano up to one year in prison or a fine for men who dress or behave as women; 2025 Kano sentence of a TikToker to one year in prison). The article cites trans-specific coverage ('I feel invisible': The challenges of being trans in Nigeria, Timinepre Cole) but contains no trans-prisoner housing or placement information for Kebbi or Nigeria.

records.current_summary:
No trans-specific incident, statute, enforcement action, or institutional statement was found for this province; the dossier states that this province (with one other) has 'no trans-specific source at all'. For a visitor, the practical exposure is the national violent-crime baseline plus the township-and-rural customary-authority axis: a visibly gender-nonconforming person outside the metro civil-society belt is more likely to encounter a chief's moral adjudication through the parallel customary-court system than a magistrate's court, especially outside the main cities. There is no province-level ban, no enforcement against expression, and no religious criminal law.

The national court's 2023 invalidity of the traditional-leadership legislation, with the declaration suspended while a replacement is prepared, reduces but does not eliminate that parallel-system concern for a traveller in rural areas. Recent severe gender-based-violence killings of women and girls in the metro drew arrests after each incident - a functioning, if strained, state-response signal - and none of the victims is identified as trans; the killings are context for local violence levels, not a trans finding.

prison_adds.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others, Case No. 2024/070075 - High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division, Johannesburg (Fisher J), judgment of 10 November 2025
prison_adds.summary: National placement standard governing trans prisoners in every province including Eastern Cape: the judgment records that DCS agrees that, under the regulations to the Correctional Services Act relating to accommodation of vulnerable inmates and the DCS Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), inmates should be accommodated in cells appropriate to their gender identity where feasible and safe; DCS further conceded its own SOPs prescribe single-cell accommodation for transgender inmates. The Equality Court, applying these instruments, ordered the DCS to accommodate the complainant in a single cell or in the same cell with inmates of the same gender identity. This is the operative rule for where trans prisoners are housed in Eastern Cape correctional centres (e.g., St Albans, Mthatha, East London), no province-specific trans-placement case being on record.

records.current_summary:
Gauteng — the province containing Johannesburg and Pretoria — is where the country's protections are most visibly operational. It hosts the first representative quantitative study of hate crimes against gay and lesbian people ever conducted anywhere in this country (2003/04, by an LGBT well-being institute with a university applied-psychology centre, documenting prevalence, consequences and contributing factors, with the era's leading community organisations as partners). A 2016 national campaign review confirms only three such studies exist in the country's history, placing Gauteng squarely in the small tier of provinces where the evidence, reporting channels and NGO capacity demonstrably exist. There is no province-specific ban or enforcement action here: the national constitution enumerates sexual orientation, and the equality statute and hate-crime framework operate uniformly, with the courts, prosecutors and civil society that apply them most concentrated in this province.

One caveat cuts both ways: the province's comparatively high recorded hate-crime volume — the very reason the evidence exists — may partly reflect better reporting infrastructure rather than greater danger. The operational conclusion stands either way: an incident a visitor reports here is likeliest to meet a functioning institutional response.

prison_adds.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others, Case No. 2024/070075 - High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division, Johannesburg (Fisher J), judgment of 10 November 2025
prison_adds.summary: The only documented determination of where trans prisoners are housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving life, is held at Johannesburg Correctional Centre: initially housed in Medium A section where she could express her gender identity (long hair, makeup, women's clothing); later transferred to Medium C section; at the time of the judgment she was housed in C Single Section, a segregated/solitary-confinement unit of Medium C, and - despite requesting a single cell - was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates (first two cisgender gay men, then one cisgender male), which DCS justified by overcrowding. The court found the DCS's SOPs prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where feasible and safe and that no basis existed for refusing single accommodation, ordering DCS to house her in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and to enforce its transgender-inmate SOPs.

prison_adds.title: Media Statement: National Preventive Mechanism welcomes the High Court ruling affirming the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities
prison_adds.summary: SAHRC (as South Africa's OPCAT National Preventive Mechanism) welcomes the 10 November 2025 judgment of the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Case No. 2024/070075), which found the DCS engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of transgender inmate Nthabiseng Mokoena - including by failing to provide appropriate accommodation - and ordered the DCS to enforce its SOPs on transgender inmates and house her in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity. Confirms the Correctional Services Act vulnerable-inmate accommodation framework as the operative housing standard in Gauteng's correctional centres.
